doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
title: Irving Kratka, Music Minus One and becoming a revivalist
summary: He claims the Music Minus One idea for Kratka and says he is an old revivalist who loved early jazz records in the Brooklyn Tech Jazz Society.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Oh there’s many things. And I have sort of a historical and scientific — not deeply historical because I love history, it was my favorite subject in school. But I remember the little details. I’m an encyclopedia about pulling teeth. I connect one thing to another and I love that every tub thing. Because it carried all the way through to Louis Armstrong you know. So anyhow, that was in Trenton. I’m trying to think — there’s a guy named Irving Kratka, played the drums. He started a record label, what was it?

It was, yeah. I started a record company with him and then, well it’s too long a story. But I made a list of possible ideas for a small record company that the big ones aren’t doing so much, and that was one of them. I mean who would have known? I mean he actually followed it through, but it was something a small company could do that bigger ones don’t. So anyhow the music continues and you know I still consider myself a musician, I mean that’s what I’ve been doing for the sole of my existence for a long time now. And I am odd in that my generation usually by this time has been playing bebop for a long time. You know, and they sort of came up in the late big band era, playing saxophone or something in a big band and then went on, you know, and the lingua franca of the day was bebop. You know? Swing wasn’t that strong. But I didn’t come up that way. You know I’m too young to have been part of the scene in the 30s to play in the big bands, and I am an old revivalist. You know after World War II there were the moldy figs, the ones that were interested in old records and King Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton and that kind of stuff, you know going back to the original. That was me. I loved that. And so in high school I belonged to the Brooklyn Tech Jazz Society and we’d bring in records and I junk shopped you know, and nothing was available, Monk. Today it’s like the computer — you can get everything, even that Red Hot Jazz Archive you can go on, you know that?
